title: Forest garden: the shrub layer
subtitle: Choosing fruiting and supporting shrubs for the 0.5 to 3 m band.
excerpt: The shrub layer in a forest garden fills the space between the canopy and the ground with fruiting shrubs, nitrogen-fixers, and hedging plants. Good choices in the UK include currants, gooseberry, elder, and sea buckthorn.
sourceNotes: Species selection after Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). Nitrogen-fixing shrub information from Agroforestry Research Trust species data. RHS data used for hardiness and fruiting seasons.

glossaryTerms.definition: A plant with deep roots that draws up minerals from lower soil layers into its leaves. When the leaves fall or are cut as mulch, the minerals become available to shallower-rooted plants nearby. Comfrey and yarrow are common examples.

content.text: The shrub layer in a forest garden fills the 0.5 to 3 m height band between the canopy trees and the ground. In a UK forest garden, this is mostly fruiting shrubs: blackcurrant, redcurrant, gooseberry, jostaberry, and elder. Nitrogen-fixing shrubs fill gaps and improve fertility across the system.

Blackcurrant and jostaberry (a gooseberry-blackcurrant hybrid) do well in partial shade, which is useful under a semi-open canopy. Redcurrant and gooseberry prefer more light and work better on the sunnier edges of the planting. All four fruit in June and July.

Elder (Sambucus nigra) is a native shrub that grows fast and tolerates shade. The flowers are edible in June (fritters, cordial); the berries ripen in August to September. It spreads by suckers and self-seeds, so manage its spread if space is limited.

Sea buckthorn (Hippophae rhamnoides) is a spiny deciduous shrub that fixes nitrogen and produces orange berries very high in vitamin C. It is dioecious: you need a male and a female to get berries. It does not shade much and works on the sunny edge of the system. Hardy to H7.

Siberian pea tree (Caragana arborescens) fixes nitrogen and produces small edible seeds. It tolerates poor soil and exposure and suits the windward edge of a forest garden. Birds eat the seeds readily.
Yarrow and comfrey work at the shrub base rather than forming a full shrub. Both are
that mine subsoil minerals and return them to the surface in their leaves. Plant them between the shrubs where they can be cut and left on the ground as mulch through the season.

Plant shrubs from November to February bare-root for the cheapest stock. Space fruiting shrubs 1.5 to 2 m apart. Space nitrogen-fixing shrubs 2 to 3 m from the nearest fruit tree. In the first three seasons, annual vegetables can fill the open ground between shrubs while they establish.

Mulch a 60 cm circle around each new shrub with woodchip in the first two seasons. This suppresses competing grass and retains moisture during summer dry spells. From the third year, ground cover plants take over and woodchip mulching becomes unnecessary.
